title: DNS, IP, TCP/UDP, Ports, and TLS
description: Follow DNS resolution, compare transport protocols, and understand ports, TLS, and HTTP versions.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish Internet networking from the Web's HTTP model.
Explain recursive DNS, authoritative servers and TTL caching.
Compare TCP, UDP and QUIC and explain HTTP/3 transport.
Describe the roles of IP addresses, ports and sockets.
Explain TLS certificate checks and protection in transit.
Diagnose likely network failures using DevTools evidence.
Distinguish HTTP/2 stream multiplexing over TCP from HTTP/3 streams over QUIC under packet loss.

blocks.text: The Internet and the Web are different layers

The Internet connects networks and moves packets using shared protocols. The Web is an application system on top, commonly using HTTP. DNS, IP, transport, TLS, and HTTP solve different problems; a failure at one stage should not be diagnosed using assumptions from another.

blocks.title: A layered mental model
blocks.text: DNS resolves names; IP and routers move packets; TCP or QUIC transports data; TLS protects traffic; HTTP defines request/response semantics. Caches and reused connections mean a browser does not repeat every step on every visit.

DNS is a distributed hierarchy of records. If the browser and recursive resolver have no usable cached answer, the resolver may follow root → TLD → authoritative nameserver. The exact path depends on delegation, DNSSEC, and caching. TTL limits reuse; DNS changes are not observed by every client instantly.

blocks.code:
Browser / OS cache
  ↓ cache miss
Recursive resolver
  ↓ no usable answer
Root → TLD → authoritative server
  ↓ answer returned and cached
Browser attempts a connection

steps.title: Check caches first
steps.explanation: The browser or operating system may already know the address. A usable cache avoids an external lookup.

steps.title: Resolve the name
steps.explanation: The recursive resolver looks up the name for the client and consults the DNS hierarchy when needed.

steps.title: Attempt a connection
steps.explanation: Successful DNS returns an address, but does not prove that the server is reachable or the HTTP request will succeed.

items: TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream and handles retransmission and congestion control.
UDP carries datagrams but does not itself guarantee delivery, ordering, or retransmission.
QUIC runs over UDP, supports streams, and integrates TLS 1.3; HTTP/3 uses QUIC.
HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP; do not say all HTTP uses TCP.

blocks.text: A port helps deliver traffic to an application on a host; the number alone does not uniquely identify a global server. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. The client verifies the certificate chain and hostname, then uses traffic keys. TLS protects confidentiality and integrity in transit and helps authenticate the server, but does not prove an application is safe or replace user authorization.
HTTP/2 multiplexing still runs over an ordered TCP stream

HTTP/1.1 commonly reuses TCP connections, with browser and server behavior determining how requests share them. HTTP/2 adds streams and interleaves frames from concurrent exchanges on one connection, reducing application-level queuing and connection overhead. But that connection is still one ordered TCP byte stream: if an earlier TCP segment is lost, TCP cannot deliver later bytes to HTTP/2 until the gap is recovered. Interleaved data for several HTTP/2 streams can therefore pause together. This is transport-level head-of-line blocking; HTTP/2 multiplexing does not eliminate it. HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC over UDP. QUIC has independently ordered streams, so loss affecting one stream usually does not prevent unrelated streams from progressing, though streams whose data shares a lost packet can all wait. Congestion control and connection-level limits still apply.

blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1  -> requests share/reuse TCP connections
HTTP/2    -> stream A + stream B -> interleaved frames -> one TCP byte stream
TCP loss  -> bytes after the missing sequence gap wait for retransmission
HTTP/2    -> the parser cannot consume later interleaved frames until that gap fills
HTTP/3    -> stream A + stream B -> QUIC streams over UDP
QUIC loss -> affected stream data waits for recovery
Other independent streams may continue; congestion control still governs the connection

steps.title: Separate HTTP streams from transport delivery
steps.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes application exchanges by interleaving frames, but TCP delivers the connection as one ordered byte stream.

steps.title: Trace the loss across the TCP connection
steps.explanation: TCP must restore missing bytes before later bytes are delivered in order. Since frames for several HTTP/2 streams share that byte sequence, the HTTP/2 layer may not receive later frames yet.

steps.title: Compare QUIC stream recovery
steps.explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams. Loss blocks data that depends on the missing bytes in affected stream(s), not every unrelated stream; a packet can carry data for multiple streams, and shared congestion control still affects throughput.

blocks.prompt: Which statement best describes packet loss with HTTP/2 over TCP?

options.text: HTTP/2 removes all head-of-line blocking because each request has its own TCP connection
options.feedback: HTTP/2 usually multiplexes streams over one connection; it does not create a TCP connection for every request.

options.text: Frames from multiple HTTP/2 streams share one ordered TCP byte stream, so a missing earlier segment can delay later bytes for several streams
options.feedback: Multiplexing reduces application-level queuing but TCP's in-order delivery can still stall later bytes on the shared connection.

options.text: TCP delivers later bytes immediately and lets HTTP/2 reorder them by request
options.feedback: TCP presents an ordered byte stream to its application; HTTP/2 frame multiplexing does not bypass a missing byte gap.

options.text: HTTP/3 changes HTTP status codes so packets can be retried
options.feedback: HTTP semantics and status codes are separate from transport recovery; HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over QUIC.

blocks.explanation: Name the layer where a behavior occurs: HTTP streams, TCP ordered delivery, or QUIC stream recovery.

blocks.title: Explain an HTTP/2 stall and choose useful evidence
blocks.context: A page loads over one HTTP/2 connection. During a lossy network interval, several resources stop progressing together, while DNS still resolves and the server stays reachable.
instructions: Draw the path from browser request multiplexing through HTTP/2 frames into the TCP connection.
Explain why one missing TCP sequence range can delay later bytes belonging to more than one HTTP/2 stream.
Contrast the relevant HTTP/3/QUIC stream behavior without claiming that all congestion or packet loss disappears.
List what you would inspect in DevTools Network (protocol, connection reuse, timing, stalled requests) and what you would correlate with server/network telemetry.
State why a slow request alone is not enough evidence to conclude that transport head-of-line blocking occurred.
requirements: Distinguishes application-level multiplexing from TCP's ordered byte-stream delivery.
Explains the shared-connection stall mechanism precisely.
Describes HTTP/3 as HTTP semantics over QUIC and states the independent-stream loss behavior with its packet/congestion caveats.
Names observable browser and network evidence rather than guessing from the page alone.
Does not recommend changing HTTP version without measuring deployment support and user impact.

items: No HTTP status with a name-resolution error: check hostname, DNS, VPN/proxy, and network.
Connection refused or timeout: check port, firewall, route, and server listener.
TLS error: check hostname, certificate chain/expiry, and system clock; do not bypass verification.
HTTP 404 means a response arrived but the resource/route was not found; 401/403 concern access, 5xx concerns server failures.
CORS is a browser policy on reading a response, not a universal explanation for every network error.

blocks.prompt: What is the difference between a recursive DNS resolver and an authoritative nameserver?

options.text: The resolver looks up records for the client; the authoritative server serves its zone records
options.feedback: The resolver performs lookup work for the client; the authoritative server serves zone data.

options.text: The resolver encrypts HTTP and the authoritative server decrypts it
options.feedback: DNS and TLS have different responsibilities.

options.text: They are two names for a router
options.feedback: Routers forward packets; DNS servers handle DNS lookup.

blocks.explanation: Distinguish client-side lookup work from authoritative zone data.

blocks.prompt: Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.feedback: HTTP/3 carries HTTP over QUIC, which runs over UDP.

options.text: DNS caching can delay when clients see a record change
options.feedback: Cached answers remain usable within their TTL.

options.text: HTTPS proves an application is safe and users are authorized
options.feedback: TLS does not prove app safety or enforce authorization.

options.text: A port number is globally unique by itself
options.feedback: A port is meaningful with an address and transport.

blocks.explanation: DNS, transport, TLS and application security complement but do not replace one another.

Explain how HTTP/3 transport differs from typical HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

items: The Internet moves packets; the Web is an application system on top.
DNS uses caches or the root/TLD/authoritative hierarchy; TTL controls reuse.
TCP provides a reliable stream, UDP datagrams, HTTP/3 QUIC/UDP.
A port does not identify a global server by itself.
TLS protects traffic in transit but does not replace app authorization.
DevTools helps distinguish DNS, connection, TLS, HTTP, and browser-policy failures.
HTTP/2 multiplexes exchanges but still shares TCP's ordered byte stream; HTTP/3 uses QUIC's independent streams, with packet and congestion caveats.
